A 38-year-old male visits an addiction medicine specialist following a referral from his primary care
physician. He reports daily oxycodone use due to persistent cravings and notes needing higher doses
to achieve the same effect. He admits to using oxycodone before driving to work and has missed work
on several occasions due to falling asleep at home, as well as failing to meet important deadlines. He
describes experiencing abdominal cramping, diarrhea, and vomiting during brief periods when he ran
out of opioids but denies any current nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain. His vital signs are normal,
and he is alert, oriented, and responsive. Physical examination, including cardiopulmonary and
abdominal assessments, reveals no abnormalities. What is the most likely diagnosis? Answer Choices:
(A) Chronic opioid intoxication (B) Severe opiate use disorder (C) Substance-induced sleep disorder
(D) Opioid withdrawal (E) Early remission from opioid use disorder (F) Tolerance without dependence
(G) Acute opioid intoxication (H) Mild opiate use disorder (I) Moderate opiate use disorder (J)
Opioid-induced mood disorder
 A. Acute opioid intoxication
B. Opioid withdrawal
C. Substance-induced sleep disorder
D. Tolerance without dependence
E. Moderate opiate use disorder
F. Opioid-induced mood disorder
G. Early remission from opioid use disorder
H. Mild opiate use disorder
I. Severe opiate use disorder
